name: Rosa Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Great. I like this kind of thing. I've got a spreadsheet for basically every decision in my life, so thinking out loud about the future is my idea of fun.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a grader and sometimes the water cart at the Saltbush lithium mine. The grader keeps the haul roads smooth so the big trucks don't wreck their tyres, and the water cart sprays the roads to keep the dust down. I'm still learning the grader; getting the right crown on a road, the slight hump in the middle so water runs off, takes a feel I don't have yet. I like that it's a puzzle, and I listen to podcasts on the water cart. What wears me out is the heat in summer and the same three roads every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still worth learning the tools. Even if AI is mostly hype, the bits that work save time. I'd probably post a little thread about how I actually use it, because people either think it's magic or useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it'd be a bit of a let-down, but fine. I've got a drone licence and I do weekend survey jobs for farmers, measuring dams and stockpiles. I use AI to process the photos and write the reports. That keeps going either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep grading, get signed off properly. Grow the drone work to two weekends a month, maybe buy a better drone with about 3,000 of my savings once I've got enough repeat customers. And keep using AI every day for the reports and quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the drone work. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A farmer at the pub was moaning that a surveyor wanted a fortnight's wait and a big fee to measure his dam. I said I'd do it on Saturday for a box of drinks and fuel money. Now I've got eleven farmers in my phone and a business name my sister came up with in the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the mine know about the side business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I told my supervisor. He actually asked me to fly the stockpile once when their regular guy was sick. That's the dream, honestly: the mine paying me for the drone stuff.

S0.say: I'd say it's still worth learning the tools, because the bits that work save time. I'd post a short thread on how I actually use AI, since people think it's magic or useless.
S0.think: Privately it would be a bit of a let-down but fine, since her weekend drone survey work for farmers, with AI writing the reports, keeps going either way.
S0.do: Keeps grading and gets properly signed off. Grows the drone survey work to two weekends a month and may spend about 3,000 of savings on a better drone once she has repeat customers.
S0.quote: Now I've got eleven farmers in my phone and a business name my sister came up with in the car.
S0.fieldNote: She has already built a small side business from a chance pub conversation, and AI is part of how it runs. She finds the plateau dull rather than reassuring. Her spreadsheet habit shows up in how she weighs every choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news if you're willing to learn, and tough if you're not. I'd try to say that kindly, because I know people on my crew who'd hear it as a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's my moment, honestly. Saltbush is a new mine and they'll automate the roads early. Somebody has to tell the robot grader where the road goes, and I'd like that somebody to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask straight away to be put on any automation trial, and do the mine's training on the fleet system. I'd keep the drone work going and push it towards the mine, offering to do stockpile surveys. If Saltbush didn't move fast enough I'd apply to the newer lithium projects that are building automated from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Maybe a little guilty when I think about the older guys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bruce, who taught me the grader. Thirty years of feel in his hands. If they automate the roads, his feel for a crown goes into the software and he goes out the gate. That bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the company to pay people like Bruce to train the system, properly, not as a favour. I don't think it's the company's job to keep everyone forever, but they shouldn't take thirty years of knowledge for free either.

S1.say: I'd say this is good news if you're willing to learn and tough if you're not, and I'd try to say it kindly because some of my crew would hear it as a threat.
S1.think: Privately I think it's my moment, since a new mine will automate the roads early. Someone has to tell the robot grader where the road goes, and I want it to be me.
S1.do: Asks at once to join any automation trial and does the mine's fleet system training. Keeps the drone work and pitches stockpile surveys to the mine, and applies to newer automated lithium projects if Saltbush is slow.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with some guilt about older colleagues.
S1.quote: Somebody has to tell the robot grader where the road goes, and I'd like that somebody to be me.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady disruption as an opening and has a clear target role. Her concern for her mentor Bruce is genuine and turned into a practical idea: pay experienced workers to train the system. Her centrist streak shows in balancing company duty against fairness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, fast, and don't wait for anyone to tell you what to do. And I'd say the government needs to be paying attention, because a lot of people aren't like me and can't move quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think even my plan has a short shelf life. If AI can survey, process and write the report, my drone business is just me holding a remote for a robot that doesn't need me. Two years might buy me one good run, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into making money while the window's open. Chase the automation commissioning jobs at new mines, which pay well and need people for a while. I'd stop the drone upgrade and save the cash instead, and I'd move anywhere for the right contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually the one who's ahead, and this is the first time I can't see where ahead is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move anywhere. Does anything tie you down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dog, Pickle, and my sister, who's an hour away. I'd take a contract on the other side of the country as long as the dog can come. My sister would understand, she always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the steady picture you said this was your moment. What's different here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Speed. In the steady one, being early makes you valuable for years. In this one, being early makes you valuable for months. I'd still do it, but I'd be doing it to build a cushion, not a career.

S2.say: I'd say get ready fast and don't wait to be told what to do. The government needs to pay attention, because many people can't move as quickly as I can.
S2.think: Privately even her plan has a short shelf life, because AI could survey, process and write the report without her. Two years might buy one good run, not a career.
S2.do: Chases well-paid automation commissioning jobs at new mines while the window is open. Drops the drone upgrade to save the cash and moves anywhere for the right contract, dog included.
S2.feel: Anxious, because for once she can't see where ahead is.
S2.quote: I'd take a contract on the other side of the country as long as the dog can come.
S2.fieldNote: Her confidence wobbled here for the first time, and she put it precisely: being early buys months, not years. She would still move quickly but for money, not a career. Her ties are light, a dog and a sister an hour away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a real move, so make it now. I'd probably run a little workshop for people at the mine on using the AI tools, if they'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd do well for three or four years, and then I'd need whatever comes after. Five years is enough to build some savings and a skill that's at least next to the robots, not under them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the automation team at Saltbush or a new mine within a year. I'd study part-time for a diploma in mine surveying, because surveyors design the roads the robots follow. The drone business I'd keep small, mostly for the farmers who've stuck with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a useful way. It gets me moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the farmers if the business isn't the future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they took a chance on me. Old Mr Hartley paid me in eggs the first time and told everyone at the cattle sale I was good. I'm not dropping him for a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'next to the robots, not under them'. What does that mean for you day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being the person who checks what the machine did, not the person the machine replaced. Designing the road, checking the survey, signing it off. Until they don't need that either, which I think is later than five years.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to make a real move, so make it now. I'd offer to run a small workshop at the mine on using the AI tools.
S3.think: Privately she'd do well for three or four years and then need whatever comes next. Five years is enough for savings and a skill next to the robots, not under them.
S3.do: Joins an automation team at Saltbush or a new mine within a year and studies part-time for a mine surveying diploma. Keeps the drone business small for loyal farmer customers.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a way that gets her moving.
S3.quote: Old Mr Hartley paid me in eggs the first time and told everyone at the cattle sale I was good.
S3.fieldNote: Her phrase about being next to the robots rather than under them sums up her strategy. Loyalty to the first farmer who trusted her overrides her spreadsheet logic. She thinks supervisory work outlasts five years but doesn't claim to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent runway, so use it. Learn now, and don't bet your whole life on one job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be okay. I'd be thirty-seven, with a surveying qualification, some savings and probably a few years running automated fleets. That's a decent hand to play when it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, I'd start the surveying diploma part-time and keep grading. I'd grow the drone business properly and buy the better drone, since there'd be years to pay it off. I'd start putting a bit into an index fund every month, maybe 150, so I own a slice of whatever comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A good kind of nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a decent hand to play. What would you actually be doing when it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, no idea. Maybe running the drone and survey side for several mines, maybe something that doesn't exist yet. The plan isn't to know the answer, it's to have enough options that I don't need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you feel worse about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the people who run things use the ten years to argue instead of plan. I can sort myself out, but the town can't if no one's organising it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a decent runway, so use it. Learn now, and don't bet your whole life on one job.
S4.think: Privately she'd be okay at thirty-seven with a surveying qualification, savings and years running automated fleets. That's a decent hand to play when AGI arrives.
S4.do: Starts a part-time surveying diploma while grading and buys the better drone to grow the business. Puts about 150 a month into an index fund to own a slice of what comes.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, a good kind of nervous.
S4.quote: The plan isn't to know the answer, it's to have enough options that I don't need to.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she relaxes back into building. She is honest that she doesn't know what she'd do at the end and frames options as the point. Her only real fear here is about leaders wasting the time, not about herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm usually fine because I'm quick, and that's the one where quick doesn't help much. What would help is clear information from the mines about their automation plans, so people can see what's coming, and cheap part-time courses for shift workers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about shift work. Every course in the world is useless if it's on Tuesday nights and you're on a two-week night roster.

headlineQuote: Every course in the world is useless if it's on Tuesday nights and you're on a two-week night roster.
portrait: Rosa Olsen is 27 and drives a grader and water cart at the Saltbush lithium mine, still learning to get the crown of a road right. She is single, has a dog called Pickle, and runs a small weekend drone survey business for local farmers, using AI every day for the reports. She plans with spreadsheets and sees automation as something to get close to. She stays calm through the plateau and steady pictures, becomes anxious when AGI in two years shrinks her head start to months, and with five or ten years plans a move into mine surveying while keeping the drone work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it's the one picture where being quick doesn't help much.
whatWouldHelp: Clear information from mines about their automation plans, and cheap part-time courses that fit shift workers' rosters.
